items.title: Bobby Johnson Jr. interviewed by Monk Rowe, Ellenville, New York, June 23, 1998
items.q: But I stayed with him a long time, and he paid me very well, Erskine did. I did all right with that band.

ctx.x: In Pensacola. Some people have a different word for it, you know what I mean? Because there was always a lot of females around, a lot of booze and everything. And they stayed with us. So when I came to New York they’d already, they were on top. They had played the Savoy Ballroom, and I was with, maybe you haven’t heard of this band, one of the great bands of our time, I was with the Don Redman Band on Broadway at the Cafe Zanzibar. And we closed one night, closed on a Sunday. And they had heard of me. They knew…

great trumpet players of our time, his name is Dud Bascomb, he was the one who made that trumpet solo in “Tuxedo Junction” with the Erskine Hawkins Band. So I stayed for a week, and the Savoy Ballroom, the money was very — the scale I think was only like $39 or something like that. So I stayed, and the guys began to like me. And as you know, Erskine’s band never integrated. We never had — we never — and that was one of the things that really hurt me. We never had any people of color in that band, but I stayed…
Can you tell me about that recording session that you did “Tippin’ In?”
